guide-overview-text:
Eating well
A full stomach is not the same as a good diet

Every food now carries real-world nutrition: calories, protein, carbohydrate, fat and fiber, four fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E and K), vitamin C, the B vitamins, and three minerals (calcium, iron and potassium). Hold a food to see what one portion of it contains, or a bowl or pie to see what one serving contains.

Your body keeps a reserve of each of these fourteen nutrients. Eating fills them and everyday life uses them up. Open the character screen (characterdialog) to see them under Nutrition, where the five food group bars used to be. Hover over a bar to see how many days that reserve would last. Typing /nutrition in chat lists them all.

Satiety works as it always has: it decides whether you are hungry, and running out of it still means starving. The reserves show whether what you eat is any good. A stomach full of bread keeps you alive, but it won't keep your vitamin C up.

While nutrient tracking is on, the five food group bars and the bonus health they gave are switched off, so only one nutrition system runs at a time. For now the reserves only keep score; the effects of a good or poor diet will arrive in a later version.

Read on: nutrient reserves, how food is counted and what each nutrient does.
guide-reserves-text:
Nutrient reserves
Measured in days

A reserve is measured in days of supply. 100% is one day's need, so a reserve of 250% lasts two and a half days if you stop eating that nutrient altogether.

Daily needs
Calories 2,500 kcal, protein 55 g, carbohydrate 300 g, fat 80 g and fiber 30 g. Vitamins and minerals use the adult daily values printed on real food labels.

Using it up
Vitamins, minerals, protein, carbohydrate, fat and fiber each use up one day's worth per in-game day, awake or asleep. Calories burn as fast as your satiety does: standing still burns about 700 kcal a day and moving all day about 2,800, while sprinting, the cold and anything else that raises your hunger rate burn more. Calories keep burning even while a good meal holds your satiety bar still. Nothing is used up in creative mode or while you are logged out.

How much the body can store
• Vitamins A, D, E and K: up to 25 days. A new character starts with two weeks' worth, so running low takes a long time, and so does recovering.
• Calcium, iron and potassium: up to 10 days. A new character starts with a week's worth.
• Vitamin C, B vitamins, protein, carbohydrate, fat and fiber: a day and a half at most. A new character starts with one day's worth, so these are the first to run low.
• Calories: up to 5 days, a modest store of body fat. A new character starts with 2 days' worth.
Anything eaten past a full store is lost.

See also: how food is counted.
guide-counting-title: Complex Nutrition: How food is counted
guide-counting-text:
How food is counted
Every ingredient counts

Single foods
Each food has the weight of a real-world portion, and its nutrition comes from real food data for that weight. Spoiling food gives less satiety and fewer nutrients in the same measure; rot gives nothing.

Meals
A serving from the cooking pot counts as the sum of its ingredients. Cooking makes food easier to digest but destroys some vitamins: a cooked meal gives about 20% more calories and carbohydrate, but half the vitamin C and three quarters of the B vitamins of its raw ingredients. Pickles and other crock contents count as they are.

Pies
A pie counts as its whole filling and crust, and each slice is a quarter of it. A charred pie has lost most of its value.

Drinks
Juice, milk and other drinkable liquids count by the litre, so a sip counts for a sip.

Large meals
The body can only take in so much at once. Food eaten within an in-game hour of the last bite counts as one sitting. In one sitting, up to a day and a half's worth of each nutrient is taken in fully. Beyond that, each extra mouthful counts for less: a further full day's worth adds only about two thirds of a day. Spreading rich foods out, and eating a mix of them, works better than one big feast.

Foods from other mods
Foods without nutrition data of their own are estimated from their food group and satiety. Their tooltip says so.

See also: what each nutrient does.
guide-nutrients-text:
The fourteen nutrients
What they do and where to find them

Calories: energy for everything you do. Densest in fat, butter, honey, nuts and bread.
Protein: builds and repairs muscle. Meat, fish, cheese, soybeans and peanuts.
Carbohydrate: quick fuel. Grains, bread, honey and cassava.
Fat: slow fuel, and needed to take in vitamins A, D, E and K. Animal fat, butter, walnuts, peanuts, cheese and sunflower seeds.
Fiber: keeps digestion moving. Flax, rye, soybeans, peanuts and berries.

Vitamin A: eyesight and skin. Carrots, butter, pumpkin and cheese.
Vitamin D: strong bones, together with calcium. Smoked and cured fish, chanterelles, morels and eggs.
Vitamin E: protects the body's cells. Sunflower seeds, peanuts and olives.
Vitamin K: lets blood clot and wounds close. Cabbage, fennel, soybeans, parsnips, blackberries and blueberries.
Vitamin C: healing, and healthy gums. Sailors who went without it got scurvy. Blackcurrants, cloudberries, bell peppers, strawberries and oranges. Cooking destroys some of it.
B vitamins: turn food into energy. Meat, fish, soybeans, peanuts and sunflower seeds.

Calcium: bones and teeth. Cheese, soybeans, milk and flax.
Iron: carries oxygen in the blood. Soybeans, morels, bushmeat, olives and amaranth.
Potassium: keeps muscles and nerves working. Soybeans, fish, cattail and papyrus roots, and peanuts.

See also: nutrient reserves.
